newsitem.title: USA: White House studiously avoids criticizing Fed.
newsitem.headline: White House studiously avoids criticizing Fed.

text.p: The White House on Tuesday studiously avoided criticising the Federal Reserve's interest rate rise, saying it respected the central bank's independence and shared its goal of solid growth with low inflation.

Issuing a statement in the name of Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin and Council of Economic Advisers Chair Janet Yellen, the White House also said it believed that the economy was poised to remain on a healthy and balanced course.

Current and former administration officials suggested the administration's muted tone reflected the influence of Rubin, a long-time Wall Street banker who is said to believe that it is counterproductive to comment on Federal Reserve actions.

"The administration recognises and respects the independence of the Federal Reserve in making decisions about the nation's monetary policy," the statement said. "We share the goal of solid economic growth with low inflation."
"Recent indicators suggest that our economy continues on a healthy and balanced course, with low unemployment, strong job creation and low inflation," the two-paragraph release added.

"We believe that the economy will continue on this path, led by strong private-sector investment which is creating a foundation for long-term growth and higher living standards for all Americans in the future," the statement concluded.

As widely expected, the Federal Reserve on Tuesday raised the fed funds rate that commercial banks charge each other for overnight loans by a quarter-percentage point to 5.50 percent, its first increase since February 1995.
The central bank left the discount rate it charges banks for money unchanged at 5.0 percent.

There is no topic of greater importance than the economy to President Bill Clinton, who won the White House in 1992 under the slogan "It's the economy stupid" and was re-elected in 1996 in part because of robust growth and low unemployment.

The White House's muted response to the Fed move was in contrast to its typical effort to exploit positive economic news, such as low inflation and unemployment figures, by having Clinton or other officials comment on them in person.

The statement made no mention of what Clinton has called his top priority, balancing the budget, a task that would grow more difficult if the economy were to topple into recession -- which few now expect -- or if rates rose significantly, thereby raising the government's cost of servicing its debt.

Officials said Rubin, who chaired the White House National Economic Council before becoming Treasury Secretary, believed rogue comments tend to make the Fed's job of keeping inflation in check even harder.
One official, who asked not to be named, told a story of Rubin once being asked to comment on the Fed. He quoted Rubin as replying: "Off the record, no comment."
The official said that the story had become a cautionary tale among administration officials about the importance of not interfering in the central bank's work.
"Anytime anyone speaks, it's over-interpreted," said the official. "I don't think anyone will comment on it beyond the written statement."
A former White House official said that the administration had sought since its first term not to roil the Fed's waters.
"We tried to maintain steely discipline in not reacting," said the former official. "People very early on realised the power of the Fed and wanted to make sure we didn't interfere."
